extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theory, constitutional law, and history (readers of Montesquieu)
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical exposition of Montesquieu's theory of governments (democracy, aristocracy, monarchy, despotism), the principles that define them, and the kinds of laws appropriate to each. Focuses on separation of powers, sources of liberty, and mechanisms that check or corrupt governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor (l'honneur) in monarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: L'honneur monarchique est le sentiment de ce que nous devons au prince, tempéré par le sentiment de ce que nous nous devons à nous-mêmes: c'est par conséquent une limite au pouvoir du prince. Il repose sur ce principe, que le prince ne peut pas tout et ne doit pas tout vouloir.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as a form of aristocratic residue in monarchies: earlier centuries' nobles (XVI) had honour that demanded fortresses and arms against the crown, whereas later (XVIII) courtly honour tolerated subservience. Honor measures the part the nobility has in government and acts as a check on princely power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion (l'opinion) as a check in monarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an opinion in a monarchy which, though not freely expressed like in democracy, exists and exerts an influence: 'the king... owes himself to the happiness of his subjects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when not legally expressed, mute public opinion causes princes to count on it; presence of public opinion (even under Richelieu/Louis XIV) distinguishes monarchy from despotism; weakening of opinion signals drift toward despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Love of liberty within monarchy via honour and opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The love of liberty can exist in a monarchy by taking the form of honour (aristocratic) and opinion (democratic); both indicate the share of nobility and people in government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two distinct principles: honour (aristocratic sentiment) and opinion (democratic principle). Their importance measures the effective participation of social groups in the State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotism defined as government based on fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotism is an abusive, low form of monarchy where citizens abandon powers to the sovereign and the government rests on fear: 'Un tel gouvernement ne repose que sur la crainte.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu/Hobbes contrast: despotism is contradictory because fear undermines the security that was exchanged for liberty. Historical/philosophical critique: despotism destroys the security it promises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for durable despotism (limits to fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: For despotism to be possible and durable, fear must not be universal or perpetual; citizens must retain private tranquillity so they do not interfere in public affairs; fear should be reserved for those who resist the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If fear is total and constant, subjects would have no reason to submit. Otherwise the regime relies on habit, respect, and other principles to moderate fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit, respect, and religion as supports of despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond fear, obedience in despotism becomes habit; subjects born into despotism may feel admiration and respect for sovereign; religion often mixes in, making the monarch sacred and increasing obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples drawn from Eastern monarchies and Manou's doctrine; religion both strengthens obedience and can act as a limit on the prince (Montesquieu: religion corrects the Turkish constitution a bit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy as republic for nobles and monarchy for the people
rubrics_metrics.description: In an aristocracy the nobles relate to each other as in a republic (love of liberty and equality among nobles), while the people experience the nobles as a monarch; thus aristocracy partakes of both republic and monarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristocracy requires noble virtue (love of state over personal grandeur), obedience to laws, avoidance of corruption; if few families dominate it becomes oligarchy; moderation is a principle of aristocracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue in different regimes (character of aristocratic vs democratic virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is necessary in aristocracy and democracy but differs in character: democratic virtue is modest, simple (sobriety, economy, love of work); aristocratic virtue has pomp and elevation and is closer to 'honour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: virtue of Dutch republic and early American republic as democratic virtue; aristocratic virtue corresponds to pride and grandeur, fitting noble preeminence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation as principle of aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristocracy can rest on moderation: balance between noble independence and people's repose; moderation prevents drift toward oligarchy or monarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as one of many intermediary forms between oppressive oligarchy and liberal aristocracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: laws relative to nature versus laws relative to principle
rubrics_metrics.description: For each form of government, there are laws that derive from its nature (institutional arrangements) and laws that derive from its principle (moral/social rules necessary to sustain the principle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu enumerates both kinds for each government (democracy, aristocracy, monarchy, despotism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy — laws relative to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Essential laws: fix the number of citizens forming assemblies; laws regarding magistratures (the people appoint magistrates); use of sortition (suffrage by lot); publicity of votes; direct legislative power attributed to the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu thought largely of ancient republics; author notes that merit may be considered in modern democracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy — laws relative to principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws to conserve virtue and equality: agrarian laws and measures limiting transmission of property; small size of inheritances; sumptuary laws and severe censure to maintain old moeurs and frugality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These laws are indispensable to preserve the frugality and virtue that sustain democracies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy — laws relative to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional laws: election by choice; a senate governing made up of nobles; provision for a dictatorship to restore principles when needed; some share of influence given to the people; grandeur of magistracies compensated by their short terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These arrangements reflect aristocracy being a republic for nobles and require mechanisms to prevent oligarchic permanence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristocracy — laws relative to principle (negative constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle-based laws are mostly negative: no personal prerogatives or privileges (exemptions from taxes), prohibition of commerce for nobles, rigorous justice for the people; also: no confiscations, no agrarian laws, no abolition of debts, no droit d'aînesse, no substitutions, no retrait lignager.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These prohibitions seek to prevent abuses that would destroy equality among nobles and protect the people's rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy — laws relative to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional features for monarchy: existence of a nobility; existence of a clergy; existence of a deposit of laws held by an independent judicial body (a 'dépôt de lois').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu values intermediate corporate bodies (parlements) as depositaries of laws; monarchy without such intermediaries tends toward despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monarchy — laws relative to principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle-based laws include substitutions (entails) that keep property in a family, retrait lignager (restitution of lands to family), privileges of noble lands, and droit d'aînesse (primogeniture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These legal mechanisms maintain the social hierarchy and the linkage between noble dignity and landed estates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotism — paucity and form of laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotism barely has laws; fundamental institutions include a vizier, sovereign army, lack of fixed succession law (prince chooses successor); practice of confiscation, exagerrated usury, peculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wars are conducted in their natural fury; religion has great influence and acts as an added principle of obedience in despotic regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Power arrests power' / separation of powers as guarantee of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: A constitution is free when no one can abuse power; this requires limits on power and that 'the power arrests the power' — separation into legislative, executive, and judicial functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu derives liberty from the distribution of powers and the mutual checking of powers; examples and references to Aristotle, Locke, and the English constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale for separating legislative and executive
rubrics_metrics.description: If the same person or body makes and executes the laws, they can create tyrannical laws to be executed with force; separation prevents arbitrary seizure of liberty and property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies equally if the people in assembly retain both powers; even popular sovereigns can oppress minorities — separation remains necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence and danger of uniting judging with other powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to judge must be independent; if joined to legislative or executive it makes the judge a legislator or an oppressor capable of destroying citizens by general or particular wills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice should be entrusted to an independent magistracy drawn from the body of citizens, who have no interest in power and therefore not in iniquity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jury idea: making judicial power 'invisible'
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of judging should not be entrusted to a permanent senate or special body but to persons drawn from the body of the people (the jury), so that judicial power becomes 'invisible' and not continuously before the eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu's explanation: jury prevents a constant visible magistracy; fear is of magistracy, not magistrates. Jury reduces the appearance of a separate ruling caste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for intermediate corporate bodies (corps intermédiaires)
rubrics_metrics.description: A medium power composed of privileged bodies (nobility, parlements) situated between executive (king) and legislative (people) unites and moderates the two, allowing mutual checks and preservation of privileges proportional to advantage in the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These bodies act as depositaries of laws and provide reciprocal veto-like functions; Montesquieu defends privileges of seigneurs, clergy, nobles, and cities as stabilizing influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and critique of Montesquieu's formulation of liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Montesquieu: 'Liberty consists in being able to do what one ought to will, and not being constrained to do what one ought not to will' and 'freedom is the right to do everything permitted by laws.' The author critiques that this restricts liberty because laws themselves can be tyrannical; law should derive from right, not the reverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes civil liberty (use faculties so long as they don't harm others, with necessary sacrifices for public safety) and political liberty (set of guarantees that ensure natural liberty will be preserved by laws).

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger that the people as legislator can become oppressive
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the legislative power is the people, the people can enact unjust laws against minorities, the rich, or religious groups; therefore absolute power of the people is not equivalent to freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemblies can devolve into oligarchies via committees that become real sovereigns (example: Long Parliament); necessity of institutional constraints and separation even in popular governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of degeneration toward despotism
rubrics_metrics.description: Destruction of intermediate privileges and corporate bodies, centralizing the State in the person of the prince, and making the capital and court the whole State lead a monarchy to degenerate into despotism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples and allusions (Tsin and Soüi, M. Law, Richelieu, Louis XIV) used as warnings: removal of pre-rogatives converts moderate states to despotic or popular states.
